title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: linking the past to today

questions.prompt: Marwa says: "I started working at the port in 2020. I still work there today." Which single sentence says exactly the same thing?

options.text: I have worked at the port since 2020.
I work at the port since 2020.
I worked at the port in 2020, and then I stopped.
I have worked at the port two years ago.

questions.explanation: "I have worked at the port since 2020." is right: a situation that began at a named point and is still true today takes the present perfect, and since introduces that starting point. "I work at the port since 2020." puts a present simple beside since, the most frequent mistake with this structure, because a present simple cannot reach back to 2020. "I worked at the port in 2020, and then I stopped." says the opposite of what Marwa means, since her work is not over. And "I have worked at the port two years ago." places ago, which dates a finished moment, next to a present perfect that accepts no date at all.

questions.prompt: Three of these sentences describe a situation that is still true today. Which one describes a situation that is over?

options.text: Amel has taught in the same school since 2014.
Amel has known her neighbours for eleven years.
Amel taught in the same school for eleven years.
Amel has lived in the same street since her childhood.

questions.explanation: "Amel taught in the same school for eleven years." is the finished one: it is a past simple, so the eleven years are closed and Amel no longer teaches there. The three others are present perfects, and a present perfect keeps the situation alive up to now — "Amel has taught in the same school since 2014." and "Amel has lived in the same street since her childhood." both start from a point and reach today, and "Amel has known her neighbours for eleven years." measures a length of time that is still running. Notice that for appears twice here with two different tenses: the marker decides nothing, only the tense does.

questions.prompt: Skander is asking his father to let him join a summer course in Sousse. Which sentence expresses his wish in correct and polite English?

options.text: I want join the summer course in Sousse.
I like to join the summer course in Sousse every year.
I'd like joining the summer course in Sousse.
I'd like to join the summer course in Sousse.

questions.explanation: "I'd like to join the summer course in Sousse." is right: I'd like is the short form of I would like, it is followed by to + a base verb, and it is the polite way to put a wish to somebody whose permission you need. "I want join the summer course in Sousse." drops the to that holds the two verbs together. "I'd like joining the summer course in Sousse." puts an -ing form after would like, which this structure never accepts. And "I like to join the summer course in Sousse every year." is correct English but says something else: it describes a habit Skander enjoys, not the permission he is asking for today.

questions.prompt: Read this story, then answer. "Habiba was fifty when her son moved to Sfax and left his old bicycle in her garage. She never learnt to ride it, and for years nobody touched it. Last winter her neighbour's daughter needed a bicycle to get to school, and Habiba lent her the old one at once. Since that day the bicycle has left the garage every single morning." What does the last sentence tell you about the bicycle today?

options.text: Habiba sold it to the neighbour's daughter last winter.
The girl still uses it every day.
It has not moved from the garage since the winter.
It stayed in the garage for years and then broke.

questions.explanation: "The girl still uses it every day." is right: since that day followed by a present perfect describes something that began at a named moment and has not stopped, so the bicycle is out of the garage today too. "It has not moved from the garage since the winter." states the exact opposite of has left the garage every single morning. "Habiba sold it to the neighbour's daughter last winter." invents a sale that the story never mentions, since Habiba only lent the bicycle. And "It stayed in the garage for years and then broke." borrows the years before the loan and closes the story with a past simple, although the last sentence leaves it open.

questions.prompt: Yosra puts this film above every other film she knows. Which sentence says that in correct English?

options.text: This is the best film I have ever see.
This is the best film I see ever.
This is the best film I have ever seen.
This is the best film I am ever seeing.

questions.explanation: "This is the best film I have ever seen." is the correct one: the frame This is the best… always calls a present perfect behind it, and ever places the experience anywhere in a life up to now. "This is the best film I have ever see." leaves the verb in its base form, although have is always followed by a past participle. "This is the best film I see ever." drops that tense altogether and pushes ever to the end, where it never stands in this frame. And "This is the best film I am ever seeing." builds a present continuous, which describes this very moment and cannot look back over a whole life.

questions.prompt: Read: "When her little grandson wrapped his arms round her neck, Leila simply melted." What does "melted" mean in this sentence?

options.text: Her feelings softened all at once.
She felt very cold and began to shiver a little.
She lost her temper and raised her voice at him.
She was disappointed and hid what she was feeling.

questions.explanation: "Her feelings softened all at once." is right: melt first describes ice turning into water, and a real-life story borrows that image for a person whose feelings suddenly soften, so that nothing resists any more. "She felt very cold and began to shiver a little." takes the verb literally and reverses it, since melting is what heat does, not cold. "She lost her temper and raised her voice at him." names anger, the opposite of the tenderness the scene describes. And "She was disappointed and hid what she was feeling." hides the emotion, whereas somebody who melts lets it show.
